turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you too, Doc. Well, I’m here because... honestly, it’s getting to the point where I keep forgetting things I really, really shouldn’t. And I don’t mean just walking into a room and forgetting why—everybody my age does that, right? I mean important stuff. Like my heart follow-up appointments. I had this issue a bit ago, and the cardiologist wanted to check in on me, you know, just to be safe and make sure everything is ticking right. Well, the day of the appointment comes and goes, completely flew right out of my head. Didn't even register. And then when they leave a voicemail about it, I tell myself, "Okay, call them back right now," but then the doorbell rings, or I decide I need to go check the mail, and boom—I completely forget to call the clinic back. It took me weeks just to get it sorted out! It’s driving me up the wall. 

And it’s not just medical stuff, it’s my day-to-day. Since I stopped working, I try to keep busy, do a little handyman work, fix things around the house, that sort of thing. But I’ll get all geared up for a repair job, walk all the way out to the shed or over to the side of the house, and realize I showed up without the right tools. I’ll be standing there looking at a loose board and realize I brought a wrench instead of a hammer, or I just brought nothing at all because I got distracted on the walk over. I have to make five trips back and forth to the garage just to do one simple job. I just... I don't know, my brain just won't hold onto what I'm supposed to be doing, and it's exhausting.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as a doorbell ringing or getting distracted while walking to do a repair job.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly reports forgetting important daily activities, such as keeping medical appointments, returning phone calls to the clinic, and remembering to bring the right tools for chores.

turns.doctor_question: Have these forgetfulness problems gotten worse compared with how you used to be?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that’s the thing, Doc. That’s exactly the thing. Have they gotten worse? I mean, yes and no? Mostly no, I think. But let me explain, because it’s not a simple yes or no. 

See, back when I was working—I was a foreman, you know, constantly moving, constantly putting out fires, dealing with this guy, dealing with that guy. My brain was always going a mile a minute, but it worked for me then. If I forgot to grab a tool, well, I was already practically running across the site to check on something else anyway, so it didn't seem like a big deal. I was always on the go, always talking to somebody, always jumping from one problem to the next. People just thought, "Oh, that’s just how he is, he’s a high-energy guy." And I was! I still am! I can't sit still for the life of me. 

But now? Now that I’m retired and just puttering around the house? It’s like all that energy doesn’t have anywhere productive to go, so the forgetfulness just... stands out more, you know? Like with the tools. I never used to just do one repair job at a time. I’d be doing three things at once. But now, I tell myself, "Okay, today I am fixing the porch railing." And then I go out there without the hammer, and my wife looks at me like I’m losing my marbles. 

So, I don’t think my brain is actually worse at remembering things than it was thirty years ago. I think I’ve always been this way—always a bit scattered, always a bit impulsive, always forgetting the little details because I’m already thinking about the next five things I want to do. It’s just that now, without the chaos of the job site to hide it, it’s a lot more obvious when I mess up. Like the cardiologist appointment. If I was working, my secretary would have reminded me, or I would have had it written on the big whiteboard in the office. Now, it’s just me and a sticky note that I probably threw away because I needed to use the pen to write down a grocery list, which I also forgot at home. So, worse? Probably not. More annoying? Absolutely. It's just... it's like a motor that won't shut off, but the car is in park. Does that make sense?

turns.patient_response:

You were just considered a handful, or a troublemaker, or maybe just a boy with way too much pep. We had these old wooden desks, the kind where the chair is attached to the desk in front of it with those heavy metal bars, and I tell you, I could never, ever just stay in my seat. It was like physical torture to sit there while Mrs. Gable—she was my third-grade teacher, strict as a board—while she was droning on about fractions or state capitals. I’d be up sharpening my pencil, or leaning over to look out the window, or just standing up for no reason at all. 

And the talking, Doc, I just couldn't keep my mouth shut. If the teacher asked a question, I didn't even think to raise my hand, I just blurted the answer right out. I can't even tell you how many notes got sent home to my parents because I was talking too much. Disruptive, that was the word they always used on those little slips of paper. They always wrote that I was a bright boy but I was disruptive.

turns.doctor_question: As a kid, did these problems ever get you into trouble at home or at school?
turns.patient_response:
Trouble? Oh, you have no idea. I mean, I sort of just touched on it with the notes sent home, but that was just the tip of the iceberg, Doc. It wasn't just a slap on the wrist here and there. It was constant. At school, like I said, Mrs. Gable and the others, they were always pulling me out into the hall. I spent so much time standing in the hallway looking at the linoleum floor that I probably knew the pattern of the tiles better than I knew my multiplication tables! They’d make me clap erasers outside, or they’d keep me in during recess—which was the absolute worst thing you could do to a kid like me, keeping me cooped up when I just needed to run. I remember one time, I was supposed to be sitting quietly reading, and I just couldn't take it anymore, so I started taking apart my pen. Just unscrewing the little cap, taking the spring out, putting it back together. Well, the spring shot across the room and hit a girl in the back of the head. I didn't mean to do it! But boom, straight to the principal's office. They thought I was being malicious, but I was just... my hands had to be doing something.

And at home? Oh boy. My dad, he was a hardworking guy, worked at the plant, came home tired. He didn't have the patience for a kid bouncing off the walls. If I interrupted him while he was watching the evening news—and I always did, because if I thought of something I wanted to tell him, I couldn't wait until a commercial break, I just had to say it right then—he would absolutely blow his top. I'd get sent to my room, but sending me to my room didn't work either because I’d just start climbing the furniture or taking apart my radio to see how it worked. I broke so many things just because I couldn't keep my hands to myself. 

My mom tried, she really did. She'd try to give me chores to burn off the energy. "Go rake the leaves," she'd say. So I'd go out, grab the rake, start raking... and then ten minutes later I'd see a cool bug, or I'd decide the rake was actually a guitar, and an hour later the yard was still a mess and the rake was left in the driveway for my dad to run over. Which he did once. Oh, the shouting that day. I just couldn't stick to the plan, you know? I’d start with good intentions, I really would. I wanted to be good. I wanted to just do what I was told and make them proud, but it was like my brain would just hijack me and suddenly I was doing something completely different, and then everyone was mad at me again. It felt like I was always in trouble for things I didn't even realize I was doing wrong until it was too late.
